title: Nim and the Dragon's Picnic
markdown:
Gadzooks! In the high rocky mountains of Misty Kettle, where the clouds often kissed the old tall peaks like gentle giants and the wind sang lullabies through the wild heather, lived a young elf named Nim. His home was a very cozy nook nestled among grey sun-warmed rocks, and it always felt like a warm hug. The air inside was warmed by the soft captured glow of sunlight, bottled and kept through the long nights. Nim’s days were usually filled with the gentle rustle of leaves in the ancient scrub, the cheerful chirping of mountain birds who sounded like tiny musical bells, and the soft comforting thudding of his very best friend, Thistle.

Thistle was not just any hare. He was a sturdy mountain hare, fur the colour of a twilight sky just before the stars burst forth. Sensitive whiskers twitched with every passing scent, from the sweet perfume of wild thyme to the earthy aroma of damp soil. Ears like velvety flags perked at the slightest whisper, whether a beetle’s scurry or the distant call of a hawk. They were as close as two peas in a well-tended pod, sharing secrets whispered on the breeze and silent understandings beneath the vast open sky.

One glorious morning, the kind where the sun seemed to beam especially for them, Nim had prepared a most wonderful picnic. Not just any picnic: a feast for the senses. Golden honey cakes, still warm from Nim’s little oven. A jug of cool dewdrop lemonade that sparkled like tiny diamonds. Plump moonberries, so dark and sweet they tasted of midnight dreams. All of it arranged with great care in a woven basket, crafted from the finest willow branches, handles smooth from years of use. Nim planned to share this glorious feast with Thistle on the Sunstone Ridge, a place where the world spread out before them like a vast painted map, colours vibrant under the high sun.

Nim hummed a little elf tune, light and airy as dandelion fluff. Thistle hopped excitedly by his side, fluffy white tail bobbing like a small cotton ball. They set off with happy hearts. But when they reached their most cherished spot, the very place always in their minds for laughter and sunshine, the basket was gone. Utterly, completely vanished, as if taken away by a mischievous gust of wind.

Nim’s berry-bright eyes widened like saucers. “Thistle.” A little ripple of worry in his usually calm spirit. “The picnic basket! It’s not here!”

Thistle’s long ears drooped. He gave a little worried thump of his hind foot against the soft earth, a familiar signal that all was not well.

Nim, though small in stature, possessed a spirit as strong and steady as the ancient mountain pines. “We must find it, Thistle.” He puffed out his chest just a little. He scanned the ground with keen elf eyes. There, near a patch of soft emerald moss, glinted a single glistening scale. Not the delicate scale of a fish, nor the iridescent shimmer of a dragonfly’s wing. Much larger, shimmering with all the vibrant colours of a rainbow that had just painted itself across the sky after a sudden storm.

“A scale! And look here!” He pointed to a peculiar large footprint pressed deep into the soft earth, a mark far too grand and deep for any badger or fox. “It seems a rather grand creature has been visiting our highlands.”

And so, with Thistle leading the way, sensitive nose to the ground, twitching whiskers mapping the subtle currents of the air, they followed the trail of unusual clues. They tiptoed through ancient woods where shafts of sunlight dappled the forest floor like scattered gold coins, turning ordinary ferns into emerald jewels. They saw where enormous clumsy claw marks had snagged the bark of ancient trees, leaving white gashes like surprised frowns. And then they heard it: the faint low sound of a deep rumbling sigh that sounded almost like the mountain itself clearing its throat after a long sleep. Nim felt a flutter of apprehension, a tiny bird of nervousness in his chest, but Thistle nudged his hand with his soft nose, a silent furry promise.

They rounded a bend where a thicket of giggling wildflowers bloomed in vibrant bursts, and there, nestled among them, was a dragon. No fearsome beast of legend. No creature of fire and fury. This dragon, whose name Nim would soon learn was Rhiannon, was enormous, yes, scales that shifted and shimmered like a mosaic of mossy stones and emerald leaves, but her eyes were large and soft, like pools of melted toffee, and she was looking at the picnic basket with a look of pure unadulterated curiosity. She held it delicately in one huge rather clumsy paw, turning it over and over as if it were a most fascinating puzzle.

“Excuse me.” Nim’s voice was surprisingly steady. “I believe that is my picnic basket.”

Rhiannon blinked, a slow majestic movement. She let out a surprised puff of smoke that smelled faintly, delightfully, of toasted marshmallows. “Oh!” Distant thunder, deep and resonant but surprisingly gentle. “Is it yours? I found it… well, I just found it sitting there, right by that patch of sun-drenched rocks, and it smelled so wonderfully of honey and berries, I simply had to investigate. I didn’t mean to take it, you see. I’m dreadfully sorry if I’ve caused any bother at all.” A single large tear, like a perfectly formed dewdrop, welled up in her toffee eye and rolled down her scaly cheek.

Nim, who was brave but more importantly kind, saw not a monster, but a very large very clumsy creature who had made a simple mistake out of pure curiosity. “It’s alright, Rhiannon.” A warm smile chased away any lingering apprehension. “We were just on our way to have a picnic. Would you… would you like to join us?”

Rhiannon’s enormous head nodded so enthusiastically that the wildflowers nearby swayed and bobbed like dancers caught in a happy breeze. Nim carefully opened the basket, its contents still perfectly preserved, and they all shared the honey cakes and moonberries on the soft yielding grass. Rhiannon’s rumbling laughter was a happy sound, a deep joyful vibration that echoed through the trees and made the leaves shimmer. She told them stories of the clouds, their shapes and their journeys, and of the secret taste of starlight on a clear night. Nim and Thistle listened, utterly enchanted, eyes wide with wonder. That is the curious thing about dragons, or at least about Rhiannon: they can be more interested in a good story and a tasty crumb than in anything else in the world.

As the sun began its slow descent, dipping below the tall mountains and casting long golden shadows that stretched like sleepy cats across the land, Nim and Thistle bid farewell to their new giant friend. Rhiannon waved a paw the size of a small boulder, genuine warmth and a little regret. “Do come visit again!”

Nim promised they would, a sincere promise under the deepening sky. Walking home, basket lighter, hearts infinitely fuller, Nim looked at Thistle. “That was quite the adventure.”

Thistle thumped his foot in perfect agreement, whiskers twitching with the happy memory of shared laughter and a dragon’s gentle sigh. They reached their cozy nook. The first stars began to prick the darkening sky like tiny welcoming lamps. Seven honey cakes with one invitation, Nim thought, and winked at Thistle, who already knew.
characters: Nim (young elf of Misty Kettle), Thistle (twilight-furred mountain hare)
